{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. It is a multi-paradigm language that guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

Memory safety means being protected from software bugs and security vulnerabilities in memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java is memory-safe because its runtime checks array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic with no bounds checking, which makes them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust began with Graydon Hoare in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first publicly released in 2010, and version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2]. Its syntax is similar to C++ [2], while its design draws on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

Rust shows that a C++-like language can offer memory safety without a garbage collector. Rust is a general-purpose language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. It is multi-paradigm and guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

Memory safety protects programs from software bugs and security vulnerabilities in memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which makes them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust began with Graydon Hoare in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first publicly released in 2010, and version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2]. Its syntax resembles C++ [2], while its design draws on functional ideas such as immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].
